prompt: What problem arises when you draw a single line-bond structure for the acetate ion, CH3CO2−?

choices.text: You must draw a double bond to one oxygen and a single bond to the other, but nothing says which oxygen is which
Carbon ends up with five bonds
choices.why: A normal line-bond structure of acetate gives every atom a valid octet; the trouble is choosing which oxygen gets the double bond.

choices.text: There aren't enough electrons to give both oxygens an octet
choices.why: Both oxygens can have octets in a single structure; the issue is that the two drawn oxygens look different.

choices.text: The negative charge can't be placed on any atom
choices.why: The charge can be drawn on the singly bonded oxygen; the question is which oxygen that should be.

explanation: A line-bond structure of acetate needs a double bond to one oxygen and a single bond to the other. But should the double bond go to the "top" oxygen or the "bottom" one? Either choice is equally good, which is the sign that resonance is involved.

prompt: Experiments show that both carbon–oxygen bonds in the acetate ion have the same length. What is it, in picometers?
explanation: Both carbon–oxygen bonds in acetate are 127 pm long, midway between a typical C–O single bond (135 pm) and a typical C=O double bond (120 pm).

prompt: What is the length of a typical C–O single bond, in picometers?
explanation: A typical C–O single bond is 135 pm long and a typical C=O double bond 120 pm. The C–O bonds in acetate (127 pm) fall midway between.

prompt: What is the length of a typical C=O double bond, in picometers?
explanation: A typical C=O double bond is 120 pm long, shorter than a typical C–O single bond (135 pm). Acetate's two C–O bonds are each 127 pm, between the two.

prompt: What do experiments show about the two carbon–oxygen bonds in the acetate ion?

choices.text: Both are 127 pm, midway between a C–O single bond and a C=O double bond
One is 120 pm and the other 135 pm, as the line-bond structure suggests
choices.why: That is what one line-bond structure would imply, but experiments show the two bonds are identical.

choices.text: Both are 120 pm, the length of a C=O double bond
choices.why: Each bond is longer than a double bond: 127 pm, partway to a single bond.

choices.text: Both are 135 pm, the length of a C–O single bond
choices.why: Each bond is shorter than a single bond: 127 pm, partway to a double bond.

explanation: Although the two oxygens look different in a line-bond structure, experiments show they are equivalent. Both carbon–oxygen bonds are 127 pm, midway between a typical C–O single bond (135 pm) and C=O double bond (120 pm).

prompt: How many picometers shorter is each carbon–oxygen bond in acetate than a typical C–O single bond?
explanation: A typical C–O single bond is 135 pm and each acetate C–O bond is 127 pm: 135 − 127 = 8 pm shorter. Each is also 7 pm longer than a typical C=O bond (120 pm).

prompt: What does an electrostatic potential map of the acetate ion show about its negative charge?

choices.text: Both oxygen atoms share the negative charge and have equal electron densities
The charge sits on one oxygen, the singly bonded one
choices.why: That is how one resonance form draws it, but the real ion spreads the charge equally over both oxygens.

choices.text: The charge sits on the carbon bonded to the two oxygens
choices.why: The map shows the electron-rich (red) regions on the two oxygens, equally.

choices.text: The charge moves back and forth between the two oxygens
choices.why: Acetate doesn't switch between forms; it has one unchanging structure in which the charge is shared.

explanation: The true structure of acetate is intermediate between the two line-bond structures, and an electrostatic potential map shows that both oxygen atoms share the negative charge and have equal electron densities (red).

prompt: What does the double-headed arrow drawn between two structures of the acetate ion mean?

choices.text: The two structures are resonance forms of the same species
The two structures are in equilibrium, converting back and forth
choices.why: Resonance forms don't interconvert; acetate has one unchanging structure, a hybrid of the two.

choices.text: One structure reacts to form the other
choices.why: No reaction is shown; both drawings represent the same ion.

choices.text: Electrons move from one structure to a different molecule
choices.why: The arrow relates two drawings of a single species; it doesn't show electrons leaving it.

explanation: The two individual line-bond structures for acetate are called resonance forms, and their special resonance relationship is indicated by the double-headed arrow between them.

prompt: What is the only difference between the two resonance forms of the acetate ion?

choices.text: The placement of the π and nonbonding valence electrons
The positions of the oxygen atoms
choices.why: The atoms occupy exactly the same place in both resonance forms; only electrons are placed differently.

choices.text: Which atoms are connected to which
choices.why: The connections between atoms are the same in both forms.

choices.text: The three-dimensional shape of the ion
choices.why: The three-dimensional shapes of the resonance forms are the same.

explanation: The only difference between the two resonance forms is the placement of the π and nonbonding valence electrons. The atoms occupy exactly the same place, the connections between atoms are the same, and the three-dimensional shapes are the same.

prompt: Which statement best describes the real acetate ion?

choices.text: It has a single unchanging structure, a resonance hybrid with characteristics of both resonance forms
It jumps back and forth between its two resonance forms
choices.why: Acetate doesn't spend part of its time looking like each form; it has one unchanging structure.

choices.text: Half of the ions have one structure and half have the other
choices.why: Every acetate ion is the same hybrid; neither resonance form is correct by itself.

choices.text: It is exactly one of the two resonance forms, but experiments can't tell which
choices.why: Experiments show the two oxygens are equivalent, so neither single form is the real structure.

explanation: Acetate doesn't jump back and forth between two resonance forms. It has a single unchanging structure that is a resonance hybrid of the two individual forms and has characteristics of both.

prompt: Where does the "problem" with drawing the acetate ion really lie?

choices.text: In representing acetate on paper: line-bond structures don't work for resonance hybrids
In acetate itself, which is unstable because it can't decide on a structure
choices.why: Acetate is a substance like any other, with one unchanging structure; the difficulty is only with the drawing.

choices.text: In the experiments, which give two different C–O bond lengths
choices.why: Experiments give the same length, 127 pm, for both C–O bonds.

choices.text: In the octet rule, which acetate breaks
choices.why: Each resonance form of acetate obeys normal valence rules; the issue is that no single line-bond drawing is accurate.

explanation: The only "problem" with acetate is that we can't draw it accurately using a familiar line-bond structure. The difficulty is with the representation of acetate on paper, not with acetate itself.

prompt: How many resonance forms combine to make the resonance hybrid of the acetate ion?
explanation: Acetate is a hybrid of two resonance forms: one with the C=O double bond to the "top" oxygen and the negative charge on the "bottom" one, and one the other way around.

prompt: What is true of the carbon–carbon bonds in benzene?

choices.text: All six are equivalent, because benzene is a hybrid of two resonance forms
They alternate between single and double bonds
choices.why: Each resonance form seems to imply that, but neither form is correct by itself; in the hybrid all six bonds are the same.

choices.text: Three are double bonds that shift position from moment to moment
choices.why: Benzene doesn't switch between forms; it has one structure with six equivalent bonds.

choices.text: All six are ordinary single bonds
choices.why: The bonds are equivalent but are a hybrid of single and double bonds, not plain single bonds.

explanation: Each resonance form of benzene seems to imply alternating single and double bonds, but neither is correct by itself. The true structure is a hybrid of the two forms, all six carbon–carbon bonds are equivalent, and an electrostatic potential map shows the symmetrical distribution of electrons.

prompt: How many equivalent carbon–carbon bonds does a benzene ring have?
explanation: Benzene is a hybrid of two resonance forms, so all six carbon–carbon bonds of the ring are equivalent rather than alternating single and double.
